assertion_audit.fails_if: Any request in the directory is never decoded, or the _read stand-in observes nothing at all; it is the positive control that makes the counts below an absence of repeats rather than an absence of decodes.

Restoring the base revision's per-call directory read gives six decodes per request and reddens this (the base arm does exactly that), and dropping the settle's second decode reddens it the other way.
Any second decode of any request fails it; 2401 is measured at base, so the guard is verified red on the reinstated regression.

A duty's kind, run id, age or reason changes, or a session's rows are attributed to another owner; the expectation comes from _base_projection's own re-read of the fixture files rather than from failure_obligations, though both sides call the unchanged _settled_state and _waited_seconds, so a defect inside those two is invisible here.
Any request is decoded twice while one index serves the sessions; it cannot fail on the publish itself, because the test builds the index rather than driving obligation_snapshot.
A second publish re-decodes a request whose file the first publish did not rewrite, or fails to decode the one it did; the expected set is the base transcription's settlement, not the head's.

assertion_independence: No assertion compares a value against the input the test itself handed the code under test. _rows/_settled_now compare failure_obligations' projections against _base_projection, which re-reads the fixture files and does not call the function under test; its use of requests._settled_state and requests._waited_seconds is a shared, unchanged predicate rather than an input echo, and is the one dependency under which the parity assertions cannot fail.
evidence_limits: No suite or mutation rerun was performed during this bounded read-only review; the scores rest on the recorded arms and the negative-control log.
The arms were read as receipts: baseline 58 passed and after 60 passed, both EXIT=0, so the added failure set is empty by construction of the two logs.
The parity assertions share _settled_state and _waited_seconds with the code under test, so a defect inside those two predicates is invisible to both sides of the comparison.
